narrative:
The model estimates a 49% chance you will leave your job, which is high enough that the company has decided to deny your promotion. This prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your work experience.

Most influential was the fact that you attended seven or more training programs in the last three years. While this might seem positive, among employees the model expected to stay, far fewer had attended this many programs. The model sees this unusually high number as a sign you may be preparing to move on.

The second strongest factor is that you have received other job offers while working here. This strongly pushes the prediction toward leaving, as most people the model expects to stay have not been approached by outside opportunities.

Third, having spent six to ten years in your current role pulls the prediction back toward staying. This is longer than most employees who are predicted to remain, and the model views your tenure as a stabilizing influence.

Taken together, the combination of extensive recent training, external opportunities, and your solid but not exceptional tenure tipped the balance just enough for the model to forecast you are likely to leave.

The organization should discuss with you whether the training reflects genuine dissatisfaction or simply a desire for growth. You may want to clarify your career goals and any external offers so the company can decide if there are ways to keep you engaged and committed long-term. (248 words)
